analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal workplace anti-discrimination law, bans forced arbitration of discrimination claims, and raises the tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Despite 151 cosponsors, the bill died in five House committees without ever getting a committee vote, and the tipped minimum wage stayed at $2.13.
analysis.plain_summary: The BE HEARD Act would have rewritten federal workplace civil rights law. It would have made discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, and sex stereotypes explicitly illegal; banned the forced-arbitration clauses that push workers' discrimination claims out of court; restricted the nondisclosure agreements that silence workers who are harassed; and phased out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage until tipped workers get the full federal minimum, plus the right to keep their tips. It also lowered the employer coverage threshold from 15 employees to 1, removed caps on damages, extended filing deadlines, and funded legal help for low-income workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — especially tipped workers earning $2.13 an hour plus tips, LGBTQ workers, low-income workers, and anyone handed an arbitration or nondisclosure agreement on their first day. The bill would also give federal agencies money to study harassment and to pay for legal help for low-income workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tipped workers and harassed or discriminated-against employees

how_it_helps.text: Phases the tipped minimum wage up from $2.13 (starting at $3.60, then increasing yearly until it equals the full federal minimum) and grants every employee the right to retain their tips.

Prohibits predispute arbitration agreements and bans contracts containing certain nondisparagement or nondisclosure clauses, so workers could take discrimination and harassment claims to court and speak publicly about them.
Makes it an unlawful employment practice to discriminate based on sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth, related medical conditions, and sex stereotypes.

Lowers the employer-coverage threshold under Title VII from 15 employees to 1, allowing a single incident to count as harassment when judged on the totality of circumstances, striking caps on compensatory and punitive damages, and extending statutes of limitations.

Requires employers with 15 or more workers to adopt and post comprehensive nondiscrimination policies and provide harassment training, and authorizes grant programs for prevention and for legal assistance to low-income workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — above all restaurants that pay the $2.13 tipped minimum, and any business that uses forced-arbitration or nondisclosure agreements to keep disputes private. Businesses of all sizes would face new policy, training, and compliance duties and increased litigation exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants and employers, especially arbitration and NDA users

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed compliance costs on many businesses: fines of up to $1,000 per violation (at least $5,000 for repeat or willful failures) for policy violations, plus mandatory interactive harassment training for employees and supervisors.

Covering employers with as few as one employee would extend litigation and compliance obligations to very small businesses, and striking the damages caps while loosening the proof standard would raise the cost of defending employment claims — costs that can be passed to customers or discourage small hiring.

Phasing out the tipped credit over several years would require restaurants to pay full minimum wage before tips, a change that would reshape restaurant pay structures and was the part most contested by the industry.
The bill would have barred using the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense in Title VII cases, a provision religious-liberty advocates opposed as going too far.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside was large: court access instead of closed-door arbitration, more time to file, uncapped damages, and a real minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs fall on employers — compliance paperwork, training, higher tipped wages, and more litigation. Some of that cost is exactly the point, since it creates a price on harassment and discrimination; the fairest criticism is the blanket coverage of one-employee employers and the litigation exposure from removing all damages caps at once, which a more targeted bill could have addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and then to two subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it; the bill never got a committee vote, let alone a floor vote, before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katherine Clark introduced the bill on April 9, 2019, joined by Reps. Pressley, Slotkin, and Mucarsel-Powell.

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — Education and Labor, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Veterans' Affairs — which meant each provision had to clear its own committee.
Two subcommittees received portions of the bill (Oversight and Investigations; Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties), but no committee ever reported it out.
151 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it.
The House never voted on the bill, and it never received a vote in the Senate; it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements kept the status quo, as did restaurants paying the $2.13 tipped minimum wage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arbitration users, NDA signers, and tipped-wage restaurants

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 151 cosponsors was a House Democrat, and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so there was no recorded roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have phased the $2.13 tipped subminimum wage up to the full federal minimum and guaranteed workers keep their tips. That industry's interest — a government-licensed tip credit letting customers' tips substitute for wages — ran against the tipped workers it applies to.

The bill would have banned predispute arbitration clauses in discrimination and harassment disputes, ending the practice of resolving those claims privately before a private arbitrator instead of in court. Millions of workers currently sign such clauses; their court access was the cost to the industry.

industries.industry: Large employers and HR/employment-defense users of nondisclosure agreements
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited certain nondisparagement and nondisclosure clauses and required public-facing anti-discrimination policies and training, with fines for noncompliance. NDAs and arbitration clauses function to keep harassment claims quiet, so the industry interest ran against workers.

industries.industry: Civil legal aid and employment lawyers
industries.note: Grant programs would fund prevention work and civil legal services for low-income workers facing discrimination. More workers would be able to afford representation.
